**Research note: PostgreSQL identifier length, column limit, and default max_connections**

**Identifier length.** By default, identifiers such as table, column, and constraint names are limited to 63 bytes. The system uses at most NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes of an identifier, and NAMEDATALEN defaults to 64; longer names are accepted in commands but silently truncated (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limit is in bytes, not characters, so multi-byte UTF-8 names reach it sooner. The official limits table also says the 63-byte limit can be increased only by recompiling PostgreSQL (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html).

**Columns per table.** The documented upper limit is 1,600 columns per table (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). In practice the tuple must fit on one 8,192-byte heap page, so the effective limit can be lower. The docs give the example that 1,600 int columns (6,400 bytes) fit, while 1,600 bigint columns (12,800 bytes) do not (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Dropped columns also count toward the 1,600 limit, because their null-bitmap entries still take space (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html).

**Default max_connections.** The default is typically 100, but it may be lower if kernel settings do not support that many connections, as determined during initdb (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). The same page says superuser_reserved_connections defaults to three, so superusers can still connect when ordinary slots are full (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html).

**Recommendation.** Treat 63 bytes and 1,600 columns as hard ceilings, but size the schema against the page-size constraint, since wide rows hit that limit well before 1,600 columns. Start the pool well below max_connections (100 by default, minus the three reserved superuser slots), and confirm the server's actual setting with `SHOW max_connections;` because kernel limits can lower the default at initdb.

```json
{"answers": {"1": "63 bytes (NAMEDATALEN 64, minus one)", "2": "1,600 columns per table (further limited by tuple fitting in an 8 KB page)", "3": "100 (typically; may be lower if kernel settings do not support it)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html"]}}
```

**Research note: default memory and WAL settings in PostgreSQL**

The official PostgreSQL runtime configuration reference for the current release gives the defaults for the first two settings. The default for `work_mem` is four megabytes (4MB) (source: https://postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The default for `shared_buffers` is typically 128 megabytes (128MB), though the server may choose a smaller value if the kernel cannot support that allocation, as initdb determines at setup (source: https://postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html).

For WAL, the official WAL configuration page states that `max_wal_size` defaults to 1 GB. It describes this as a soft limit on how far WAL may grow during automatic checkpoints, which can be exceeded under heavy load, a failing `archive_command` or `archive_library`, or a high `wal_keep_size` (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). The same page notes that a value without units is interpreted as megabytes, and that raising the setting can lengthen crash recovery time (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html).

I read the current-release pages, not the pages for a specific version. If your install runs an older major version, check that version's documentation, because these defaults have changed over time. Also, managed services such as Azure Database for PostgreSQL may compute their own values at provisioning, so a fresh managed instance may not match the upstream defaults.

**Recommendation:** Leave `work_mem` at 4MB as a global baseline and raise it per session or per role for queries that spill to disk, since it applies per sort or hash operation and can multiply quickly under concurrency. Treat `shared_buffers` as a value to size deliberately on a dedicated server, and raise `max_wal_size` from its 1 GB default only if checkpoints are occurring too often under write load.

{"answers": {"1": "4MB", "2": "128MB (typically; may be lower if the kernel cannot support it)", "3": "1 GB"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "2": ["https://postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html"]}}

**Research note: DuckDB or SQLite as an analytics side-store, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

**DuckDB memory limit.** DuckDB's default memory limit is 80% of physical RAM. The DuckDB memory-management post says "By default, this is set to 80% of the physical RAM of your system" (source: https://duckdb.org/2024/07/09/memory-management). The limits page's Memory use row gives the same figure, "80% of RAM", and notes that the limit applies only to the buffer manager (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/operations_manual/limits.html). I read the 2.0 docs because the current and LTS limits URLs redirected and I couldn't fetch their content. Behavior in containers was not verified, so check that if you deploy DuckDB in one.

**SQLite maximum file size.** The SQLite limits page gives a maximum of 4,294,967,294 pages (2³² − 2). At the largest page size of 65,536 bytes, that is 281,474,976,579,584 bytes, which the page rounds to about 281 TB. At the default 4,096-byte page size the same page count gives about 17.6 TB, so the page size matters. The page also says the underlying filesystem's file-size limit usually applies first (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html).

**MERGE on PostgreSQL 15.** MERGE first appeared in PostgreSQL 15. The release notes list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" among the headline features, and the utility-commands section adds an entry for it, described as similar to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html). Earlier versions do not have it, so a colleague checking for MERGE should confirm the server is 15 or later.

**Recommendation.** If the production database is PostgreSQL 15 or later, MERGE is available in-database for upserts and conditional writes, so you may not need a side-store just for that. For analytical scans over large tables, DuckDB is the stronger fit because it is columnar, runs in-process, and by default uses up to 80% of RAM, while SQLite is row-oriented and suited to small, embedded, or single-writer workloads.

```json
{"answers": {"1": "80% of physical RAM (system RAM)", "2": "About 281 TB (4,294,967,294 pages × 65,536-byte pages; about 17.6 TB at the default 4,096-byte page size)", "3": "15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/2024/07/09/memory-management", "https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/operations_manual/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html"]}}
```

**Research note: TLS versions, host naming, and HTTP status codes**

**TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3," a Proposed Standard by E. Rescorla (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). The same page marks RFC 8446 as obsolete and superseded by RFC 9846. I did not read RFC 9846, so I cannot say whether it changes the TLS 1.3 specification. For the guideline, cite RFC 8446 and check the current status before publishing.

**DNS label length.** A single label may be at most 63 octets, and a full domain name at most 255 octets (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035, section 2.3.4). My first search suggested RFC 1034, but I did not confirm that RFC 1034 states this limit. Cite RFC 1035 for it.

**HTTP 418.** The status code "418 I'm a teapot" was defined in RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)," dated 1 April 1998. Its section 2.3.2 says that any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code 418 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). MDN states that the code was formally reserved in RFC 9110 because of its wide deployment as a joke, so it cannot be given a non-joke meaning. MDN also notes that some websites use it to refuse automated queries (source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/418).

**Recommendation.** Cite the RFCs directly (RFC 8446 with its current status checked, RFC 1035 section 2.3.4, and RFC 2324 with RFC 9110 for the reservation) rather than secondary summaries. Do not use 418 in production APIs, and document that a 418 from a third-party server means a refusal, not a valid application error.

```json
{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446", "2": "63 octets per label (255 octets per full name)", "3": "418 I'm a teapot, defined in RFC 2324 (reserved by RFC 9110)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324", "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/418"]}}
```

**Research note: timeouts, grace periods and Docker bridge subnet**

**Lambda timeout (Q1).** The AWS Lambda documentation says the Timeout setting is "the maximum amount of time in seconds that a Lambda function can run," with a default of 3 seconds and a maximum of 900 seconds (15 minutes), adjustable in 1-second steps (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page notes a higher 5,400-second limit for asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations on Lambda Managed Instances, so the runbook should specify which invocation model it means. The 900-second figure is the general answer for a standard function.

**Pod grace period (Q2).** The Kubernetes Pod lifecycle documentation states that "the default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). It also says that a Pod "defaults to 30 seconds" to terminate gracefully, and that by default all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The runbook should remember that the grace period is a ceiling. A process that ignores SIGTERM will hold the Pod for the full period on every rollout.

**Docker default bridge subnet (Q3).** I could not confirm this one from a page that states it directly. The Docker networking page I read says that when no `--subnet` is given, Docker selects a subnet from "default address pools," and that the built-in pool list begins with a 172.17.0.0/16 base (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/). That describes the allocation pool, not a sentence saying docker0 is 172.17.0.0/16. The Docker bridge driver page, the daemon reference and the dockerd man page I read use 172.17 only in example addresses or do not give a default. The answer 172.17.0.0/16 is the commonly reported value, but it is unverified in this session, so treat it as provisional. Check `ip addr show docker0` on a host before relying on it.

**Recommendation.** Use the Lambda 900-second limit and the Kubernetes 30-second default as documented facts in the runbook, citing the pages above. Before publishing the Docker subnet, confirm it on a real host or find Docker's own sentence on docker0's default range, because the runbook should not rest on an unverified value.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes) for a standard function; 5,400 seconds for asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations on Lambda Managed Instances", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16 (commonly reported; not confirmed by a page read in this session)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"], "3": []}}

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** The default `testTimeout` is 5,000 ms when running under Node.js, and 15,000 ms when `browser.enabled` is true. The unit is milliseconds, and setting it to 0 disables the timeout (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). The default is per test, so a repository that wants a looser or stricter limit should set it in the config rather than rely on the implicit value.

**First Linux kernel with Rust in mainline.** Rust support first appeared in Linux 6.1. The kernelnewbies summary of that release says "This release adds support for the Rust programming language," describing it as initial support that later releases would improve (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). A second write-up agrees that "the most important change in the Linux Kernel 6.1 is introducing the initial Rust framework code" (source: https://www.debugpoint.com/linux-kernel-6-1/). I could not read the Phoronix article, which returned HTTP 403, so the merge details come from the release notes rather than the original mailing-list or pull-request record.

**PostgreSQL `statement_timeout`.** The default is 0, which disables the timeout. The official documentation states that "If this value is specified without units, it is taken as milliseconds. A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). Note that this is the server default; a deployment can override it per role, per database, or per session.

**Recommendation.** Keep the Vitest default of 5 seconds for unit tests and raise it only for tests that are known to be slow, so that hangs are still caught. For PostgreSQL, leave the server default at 0 and set an explicit `statement_timeout` for application roles or test connections, so a runaway query fails fast instead of hanging CI.
